title: ME.'s Eddie Reyes Talks 'ALL GOOD THINGS,' Creative Freedom And Paranormal Encounters
excerpt: PopHorror interviews Eddie Reyes, founding guitarist of Taking Back Sunday, about his new band ME. and next chapter in music.
content:
A ghost moving his coffee cup 20 feet across the kitchen doesn’t bother Eddie Reyes in the slightest. But the thought of becoming a “rock dude” again after nearly a decade away from the industry is, admittedly, a little scary.

Since 2018, which saw the founding guitarist’s departure from Taking Back Sunday due to contention in the emo scene, Reyes has been focused on sobriety, fatherhood, and his deep passions for all-things horror and paranormal. But a meeting with former TBS bandmate Mark O’Connell changed everything. As they began to resolve old conflict, their mutual love of music took its place. The result? A brand-new band ME. and debut album All Good Things.

ME., comprised of Reyes (guitar), O’Connell (drums), Mike Jansen (vocals) and Neal Amiruddin (bass), represents a deliberate fresh start and return to when pop-punk was fun. No big labels placing demands. No egos. No overthinking anything. Just complete freedom to throw anything at the wall and see what sticks.

On the heels of the album’s release, PopHorror caught up with Reyes to discuss this unexpected chapter, the refreshing mindset he and O’Connell stuck to when writing All Good Things, and some of his most memorable paranormal experiences growing up in Amityville, New York.

PopHorror: ME.’s debut album All Good Things came out this summer. How have the past few months been for you now that it’s out in the world, people are hearing it and you’re getting what seems to be really amazing feedback?

Eddie Reyes: It’s great. I’m a little bit in limbo because we’re in a hiatus for the moment, trying to figure out things about shows and stuff. I’m a little antsy to play shows, go on tour and push the record. The industry’s different now. It’s not like back in the day where you had to rush, rush, rush. Now, you put something out there, you let people feed off it and then people start sharing it. 

But if we take this on the road, I hope we’re accepted. I mean, I’m old. We’re a bunch of old guys trying to tour again and be rock dudes again. I walked away from music 10 years ago. I didn’t want to play music anymore. I walked away from Taking Back Sunday and everything. So for me, it’s a surprise that I got back into it and now I have to adjust into being a touring musician again. But I’m also trying to get everything ready. My kids are grown. My daughter’s off to college. My son decided to take a year off and then he’s going to college because he wants to see where this goes for me and help me. So it’s getting the family and everyone ready to get in that mindset again, that this might be possibly a thing where your dad’s going to be touring all the time again. 

I can’t speak for Mark, but in my opinion, I thought we were just going to get together and write a record. I have a bunch of old songs, he has a bunch of old songs. I thought that’s all it was really going to be – just me and Mark trying to fix things between us again. It’s still a difficult thing and we’re working through it, but we’re mature adults now. So it’s one of those things where it’s just happening. At first it was like, “Oh, we’re just going to record and put this EP out. Look what these old guys did with some other dudes that are friends of ours.” Now it’s like, no, people like it. 

I guess I have a bad habit of becoming part of things that people like. Maybe it’s a good thing, I don’t know. Maybe it’s just the way I write music. I don’t know how else to write. All my songs sound the same. People are like, “Oh, it’s going to sound like that band.” Well, yeah, because I started that band and wrote those songs! It’s not an ego thing because I don’t have an ego. I’m such an anti-ego person. My disorders don’t allow me to have an ego. But I’m getting back into it. It’s exciting and it’s also scary. I could have just said that instead of talking your ear off, but when you’re AuDHD, that’s what you do. [laughs]

PopHorror: Hey, sounds like the best kind of problem to have – consistently making music that people love! 

Eddie Reyes: Yeah! I’ve been doing it for a long time. My first hardcore band was ‘87, ‘88. So I’ve been doing it for a while. I’m a product of all the great bands that influenced me in the ‘80s and early ‘90s. That’s just how I write. Mark has a similar way of doing his thing and writing his songs, drum parts and whatever he comes up with. I thought I was just going to put out my last opus before I concentrate on being my son’s manager and pushing him out there because he’s a thousand times better at every instrument than I’ve ever been. But now I gotta be cool and act like a rock dude again instead of being a nerdy metalhead hardcore horror kid from Long Island, New York that just wants to go to comic stores. Now I gotta go back out there and act cool again…and I’m not cool. 

The Reunion That Started It All

PopHorror: But the nerdy side is what people connect with! Now, your son Jonas – I understand he was instrumental in helping you and Mark reconnect. What was that first meeting between you two like?

Eddie Reyes: It went well, it was just weird. I never in my life thought that would happen. Even in passing, if I was at a show, if I saw the old members, I probably wouldn’t even say hi. I like to talk about psychological stuff because I had to go through a lot. I had to go through four rehabs. I had to do this, I had to do that to clean my body, fix my brain. My doctors, therapist and sponsors all said, “When you shake off the bad seeds, you don’t want to pick them up and plant them again.” So it’s hard for me. I don’t have anything against them personally, let them live their life. They have families. Good luck, carry the band on, just send me the money that you owe me for all this work I did in starting the band. We’re all peaceful, no one’s enemies. For me, it was hard to put away a lot of stuff that I know personally happened to me. That was how things were. I don’t want to get too deep because I don’t want to give them any time. But it’s still a process of me being able to comfortably feel like I believe certain people and trust certain people again. 

I’m going through that process still. But my son was like, “I’ve been talking to Mark.” My son’s a grown man. I can’t tell him who he can’t talk to. I said, “Oh, okay.” He’s like, “Yeah, he said to reach out to him because he’d like talking to you.” I was like, “It’s been almost 10 years. It takes that?” But hey, I did it, and we started talking. Mark said, “I have a manager, would you like to talk to her? Let’s set up a meeting with Casey.” Me and my son went out to New York, met up with everyone. It was cool. I had a lot on my mind that I wanted to say, but I knew I didn’t need to say any more because I’m past that and it’s not going to make me better. It was smooth. And it’s been almost two years. There’s been some really rough times and there’s been some awesome times. It’s working out so far. But for me, it’s now more a process of going back out there and seeing faces I haven’t seen in a long time. I have people going, “Oh, you really are still around and you really are okay.” There’s a lot of processing. And then when I met up with Mark, it wasn’t as much as I thought it would be. It was a couple of apologies and that’s it. We just started talking music again. 

PopHorror: How did you guys get from that initial meeting to being in a full-on band together again?

Eddie Reyes: We went into the studio. I put down a bunch of old songs I had written that I never got to use and some new riffs that I just kept from sitting home. And Mark had some ideas and we put it all together. Then we had a contest. Mike, the minute I heard Mike sing, and his persona and character, instantly I was like, “I love this guy.” I have this way of going into a room and I could point out who sucks and who’s awesome. Coincidentally, we have the same birthday! And all the bands that inspired him are all the bands I told him to go listen to. It’s just so crazy. Everyone just clicks. Then we wrote a fucking great record and now we have to do something about it. I can’t just put it out and retire. Come on! It can’t be 15 years from now and people are like, “Hey, you ever hear this band ME.? They’re kind of like that band Handsome. They put one one great album and no one ever knows what happened to them.” I thought it was going to be like that. 

No Limitations…Just ME.

PopHorror: You’ve spoken about how you gave yourselves complete freedom with this album. Throw anything at the wall. Don’t get in your own way. No shits if anyone streams it. After spending so much of your career making music professionally under different circumstances, how did this compare? What did it unlock in you creatively?

Eddie Reyes: From past experience, it was always truly a punk rock, hardcore mentality. But then you get corporations that go, “Oh, look at this scene. It’s blowing up. Let’s make money off of these kids.” After a while, that kills the “who gives a shit, let’s just write good music, go out there and have fun” attitude. You have to write this or that now. And I was tired of that shit. That’s not me. That’s not how I grew up. Those aren’t my morals and ethics. I’m just a punk hardcore kid from New York that wants to play music, hang out with my friends, go to a diner after a show and talk about the show. Instead, it turned into, “Nope, you’ve got to write another song.” With ME., we said, “Fuck that. We’re gonna write what we want to write. If they don’t like it, don’t work with us. We’ll figure out how to put the album out ourselves.” When you’re in your fifties, you don’t give a shit anymore. It’s like, do you know how much I’ve done for this scene? Do you know how many bands I started and how many people I’ve inspired? Or, better yet, me and the 30 some other dudes in New York from the ‘80s who decided to start a scene that the whole world’s into now? Like, I’m okay to call it a day, you know? So we didn’t want to do that. 

And I’m not going to sugarcoat and say we didn’t fight a lot about this and that. There’s still a lot of things to shake off. But we went in it with that mentality and we wrote what we wanted to write. There’s no point in overthinking it. Let’s have fun doing it. That’s the attitude of ME. There’s going to be haters, including, I’m sure, ex-bandmates. But we don’t care. And that’s the point – just write some songs and try to have fun. It’s not going to be perfect, but try to have fun. 

I don’t want that taste of major labels in my mouth anymore. I don’t want that — being around fake ass people. The scene started getting fake. There’s so many industry plants. There’s so many fake bands that you have to sit there and listen to their bullshit, them telling you, “Oh, thank you for inspiring me.” Nah, you’re a fucking label plant. A label put you together to be like us. We don’t want that. We just want to put out our record, go play some shows. We don’t care. Hopefully, we can pay our bills. But if we don’t, it was fun. And that’s me speaking for myself. I don’t know how Mark or Mike feels. They probably want to be the next Elvis, who knows? I’m saying me personally. 

PopHorror: Or ME.!

Eddie Reyes: [laughs] Exactly! That’s why I named the band ME. When we were coming up with names, my son found this pin in this old thrift store down in Columbus, Ohio. It was a green pin. My son knew I was bummed out, just going through the motions. He’s like, “Here you go, Dad, check that out.” It’s a green pin with a thumbs up. It says “ME.” and then underneath it says something like, “Great self-esteem.” I always thought that was a great idea and I’ve always wanted to name something that. Coincidentally, I believe in energies and the universe. And I’m like, “This is a sign because Mark and Ed. Why don’t we just call the band ME.?” Mark was like, “That’s great.” Then Mike came in and it just all fell together. That’s how the name came to be and that’s honestly how the world got a record out of a bunch of grouchy old dudes. I’m not going to be running around on stage like I used to. I’ll probably be walking really fast, lifting one leg instead of jumping. 

Wait, so you’re a horror site!?

Horror Passions And The Paranormal

PopHorror: Hell yeah we are! Are you a horror guy? What are your favorites?

Eddie Reyes: I’m an old school horror guy. When you walk into our living room, it’s covered in horror, Star Wars and Godzilla. My favorite movie of all time will always be Dawn of the Dead, the original. My second favorite movie will always be one called Children Shouldn’t Play with Dead Things. It’s so low budget, but so creepy. I love it so much. I actually gave a copy to Frank [Iero] from My Chemical Romance because he was like, “What’s your favorite horror movie?” I was like, “Well, I can give you Dawn of the Dead, but that’s typical. I can give you this.” The way it’s done, it is so fucking creepy and dark as hell. It’s one of those movies that has a really small cult following. I wanted to name a band that – Children Shouldn’t Play with Dead Things. If we got sued, I’d change it to We Shouldn’t Play with Dead Things. It was going to be a grind core band.

I was into a lot of Italian zombie flicks in the ‘80s and ‘90s when my mom thought I was a demon. She was a Jehovah’s Witness and I’m in my room with vampires blasting black metal. But Dawn of the Dead always stuck with me as a kid. You know when you see a movie as a kid, it fucks you up mentally? That movie didn’t – it hyped me up because I have this dark sense of humor. I was like, “I hope it’s really like this if it happens.” I like all horror, but I’m not really a big horror fan of movies now because I think they’re being pushed out so fast that there’s no soul and no spirit. The last movie that was able to capture all that was Hereditary. It’s in my top 10. But after that, they’re just okay. I saw Weapons, eh. It’s like they do this whole psychological thing, hype it up and then in the end, all these movies end like that, all those A24 movies. 

PopHorror: I felt that way about Obsession. Enjoyed it, but wasn’t, well, obsessed. 

Eddie Reyes: Yes! Like, have you seen The Shining? It’s crazy. But the last great horror movie personally would be Hereditary. 

PopHorror: Does horror ever creep into your music at all influence-wise?

Eddie Reyes: Honestly, when I write the heavy breakdown parts, I imagine myself being in a death metal band, wearing a Day of the Dead t-shirt. I want to be so dark and have red lights and smoke, but then I shake my head and in reality, I’m in a room full of dorks and we’re writing melodic, post-hardcore, emo. It’s like, goddammit! One day I’ll have that evil. I want to walk out on stage with the makeup on and the lights and the fire. It’s never gonna happen. So I imagine that when I’m writing music, that I’m writing this evil, dark, horror opus. But really, it’s just wimpy. [laughs]

PopHorror: Hey, you never know – that can be the next band you start. 

Eddie Reyes: Right? ME. Part 2: The Dark Side. I would love that. Maybe I should just start another band and do strictly horror rock or something. 

PopHorror: There’s such a market for that right now. 

Eddie Reyes: Yeah, and it sucks because it took forever to become popular. And here I am, always into that stuff, and now it’s popular. But now I’m old and I don’t get to enjoy it!

PopHorror: As a horror fan, do you ever go to the conventions just as a fan of the genre?

Eddie Reyes: My wife and I, we went to a couple of cons. I literally went to a Star Wars con just to buy figures and then leave. I don’t even care about, like, “Oh, that’s Darth Vader. Cool.” Meanwhile, I’m like, “How much for that one?” My daughter’s leaving tomorrow for Renaissance Faire, she’s a Renaissance nerd. She likes LARPing. When I was in LA, I went to a really good horror con and I got to meet Bruce Campbell and all of my idols…briefly. I wanted to talk his ear off because it was the whole “I think he knows me and I know him and he’s special to me,” but then they pushed me down a line. It was that kind of meeting. When the kids are in line meeting me, I’m not going to do that to them. That was years ago, though. I’d like to go to one soon. It’s fun. You get to be yourself. You get to fucking let your autism out, man. 

And I’ve always wanted to do a horror con. When I was in my hiatus of staying away from the world and hating everyone, just rebuilding my brain, I did a lot of podcasts. I didn’t talk poorly about anybody because I’m not into that. I’m not into talking shit unless it’s facts. But I did Sasquatch ones, paranormal ones. And I’ve had my own experiences, so it was fun doing all that. I was telling my wife I should do a podcast where the subject is whatever I choose that day – horror movies, bands. Maybe I’ll still do it. 

PopHorror: Tell me more about your paranormal experiences!

Eddie Reyes: Let’s just say when I sold my house, I had to sign a waiver. It sold really quick. I guess it’s cool to own a haunted house now. I lived in a house that was built in 1858, an old farmhouse on a hill across the street from a little public golf course in the countryside of Ohio, where we live. We lived there for 15 years. My kids grew up with all the ghosts in the house. We’re not afraid of ghosts. I mean, it’s such a cliche line. Where we live now, I moved into this old building downtown in the city and it’s so haunted here, too. But she’s so sweet. The older lady next door, she said, “Oh, that’s just Rose. She lived there for 40 years. She’s a sweetheart.” True story. My son was like, “Not only did I smell her perfume, but I saw her walk down the hallway.” I was like, “Awesome.” 

Our old house was so haunted, but they were nice ghosts. My neighbor brought me the history of it and all the deaths that happened there. Just for fun, we had two separate mediums come and we didn’t tell them anything. They both told us the exact same thing. So when we sold our house, our realtor was like, “Can you sign this, too? It’s a waiver because this house is infamous.” I’m like, “Great.” But hey, it sold in two seconds. 

And I grew up in Amityville, Long Island, which is where the Amityville Horror is. So I already grew up with all the horror and hauntings and stuff in my head. I love that shit. Me and my wife all the time are like, “Did you see that?” “Yeah!” “Tell him to come and hang out with us.” I walk into places and I can sense energies. I sound like one of those crystal people, like, “Oh, the chakra.” No, fuck that. I don’t believe in any of that, but I believe in energy. I believe that this vessel, when it dies, what was looking through those eyes goes somewhere else, starts over. 

My dad, when he was alive, was always like, “It was a bear, dude. I was just messing with you.” But when I was a kid, we went camping at the upstate New York/Vermont border. Mind you, my dad barely spoke English, but he loved camping. We were fishing and in the distance, maybe 80 yards, my dad said, “Look to your right.” There was something brown in the water, like on the edge. It stood up, turned around and walked back into the woods. My dad started laughing and told me when I was growing up, “Don’t even bother telling people because no one’s gonna believe you. It was a bear, sweetie.” I was like, “Are you sure?” So all my life, I had that in my head and I swear to God, it was not a bear – that was fucking Bigfoot and it was awesome. 

I don’t believe in cryptids. I believe in Sasquatch because, of course. I don’t really believe in Loch Ness. But I believe in lores because if you believe in ghosts, you’ve got to believe in lore. You’ve got to believe in curses. And I believe in aliens because I have seen some crazy shit with people sitting next to me, and I think that’s exciting. I wish they’d come down here and fix this goddamn country already. 

PopHorror: Didn’t the government basically confirm the existence of aliens recently and we just completely brushed past that as a society?

Eddie Reyes: I’ve always known they exist. We were out in the countryside a month ago and saw three things just split apart. I could say they were drones. But the speed that they split up and took off in a perfect triangular way, it’s impossible. They’re everywhere and they’ve been here the whole time. I believe they put us here. They’re here watching us, keeping an eye on us. We’re still in this child-like state and they don’t want to do anything about it. Call me a crazy conspiracy theorist or whatever. But I’m not afraid of death. We just go on to another form of us in another universe of the same timeline. Deja vu is just a memory of your past life. I hope when I start my next life, I still have a little bit of what I learned in my later years. That I could fully be a good guy and teach everyone exactly how they should be. That’s all me in one bowl. 

Final Words

PopHorror: Looking ahead, what are your goals for ME.? What do you hope this music does for listeners, especially those who have been following you through different bands?

Eddie Reyes: Do you want some bullshit like, “I hope the world gets it and we change lives,” or honesty?

PopHorror: Honesty. 

Eddie Reyes: I’ve been doing this for so long. I’ve been in so many bands that did so many wonderful things. For me, this is another awesome thing happening in my life. I honestly just want people to take the songs, take the lyrics and make them what you want. Just enjoy it. I don’t want to sit here and say it’s no big deal, that I don’t care. I care a lot. I just want people to hear it out, man. If you don’t like it, that’s great. But at least take the time to check it out and I hope to see you at the shows. It’d be nice to talk to people again. I want to make it a point to definitely spend a lot of time with the people that come to the shows because I wasn’t really allowed to do that in my other situation. There were rules and I couldn’t really engage, actually listen to people’s stories. I want to play music, look out in the crowd and see everyone smiling. I don’t care about moshing and all that. They can do that if they want, but I just want people to come to shows, sing along and just enjoy this moment. 

I don’t know how long it’s gonna last. I don’t know how many records we’re gonna do. I just want to look out in a crowd and see everyone there with me, on the same page, having the same feelings. I hope people take these songs and make them their own personal songs, that they learn from them or they feel what Mike is singing about. I’m not looking to change anyone’s life. I’m not creating new sounds or trying to open new doors, so whatever hype is out there, that’s great. I don’t want to take it too seriously. I’m not a spring chicken anymore. Why not have fun? 

PopHorror: You can definitely hear that light-hearted energy on the album and I think it’ll translate so well on stage. 

Eddie Reyes: Yeah, we worked hard on that record. I did a lot of traveling. I was driving back to New York every month for two years. My poor car is falling apart. We’re not expecting to be the next Turnstile. I always tell my son, “You see Turnstile right now? That was your dad in 2004, 2005.” I know what they’re feeling and it’s a wonderful feeling. I’m so proud of that band, but I don’t really care about that feeling anymore. I want to go out and have fun, have laughs, play sick crowds and make a couple of bucks to pay the bills. See you guys in a month. That’s what I look forward to. It’s like the basics of being a punk rock kid growing up in the scene – go to a show, have fun, don’t overthink it, stop trying to be No. 1. 

PopHorror: Any final words for our readers?

Eddie Reyes: Listen, when I say I believe in ghosts, I really do. I’ll give you one more story. I’m at the bar at my house watching TV, drinking my coffee. I put it down. I change the channel. I go to grab my coffee. It’s 20 feet down the bar across the kitchen. Ghosts exist! 

Thanks for speaking with us, Eddie! Keep up with ME. at thebandme.com/.
